name: Egg-white and beeswax nail stains

card.summary: An ancient Chinese nail-colouring method using egg white, beeswax, gelatin and dyes to give nails colour and gloss.
card.note: Historical practice; modern polish has largely replaced it.

quick.overview:
Before modern nitrocellulose polish, nails were coloured with natural mixtures. In China, nail coloring made from beeswax, egg whites, gelatin, vegetable dyes and gum arabic is recorded for the Ming dynasty.

The appeal was the same as today's polish: coloured, glossy nails that look groomed. It is a historical practice with limited documentation.
quick.how: Per historical accounts, the ingredients were blended into a coloured lacquer and brushed onto the nails. Some revival crafters make versions today.
quick.risks: Historical recipes used natural ingredients, though dyes varied. Egg or dye allergies are a plausible concern; no documented harms were found.

lead: Egg-white and beeswax nail stains refer to historical nail lacquers made from natural ingredients. The earliest nail coloring is traced to China, with a Ming dynasty mixture of beeswax, egg whites, gelatin, vegetable dyes and gum arabic.[1]
The coating gave nails colour and shine, so hands looked polished and groomed. Royal houses used colour as a status marker; red and black later became royal favorites.[1]

chain: Egg white, wax and dye mixture applied
angle.text: The mixture works as an early nail polish, tinting and glossing the nail plate. It is chiefly of historical interest today.

paras: The Ming-era recipe combined beeswax, egg whites, gelatin, vegetable dyes and gum arabic.[1]
Nail coloring is traced to China around 3000 BCE, with gold and silver favored by the Zhou royal house around 600 BCE.[1] Elsewhere, Egyptians used henna on nails.[1]

timeline.event: Zhou royal house favors gold and silver nail colour.[1]
Recipe using beeswax, egg white, gelatin, dyes and gum arabic recorded.[1]
